look_here_first: Start with several adult leaves: chinkapin oak has an elongated chestnut-like blade with many regularly spaced teeth, each served by a near-parallel lateral vein; its sharp/forward-pointing teeth have NO red-oak terminal bristle. Turn over the leaf for a pale, minute stellate-hairy surface, and confirm a moderately sized acorn in a NON-fringed cup. Compare bur oak's midleaf waist and shaggy cup.

project_inclusion.range_basis: Kew/POWO accepts Quercus muehlenbergii and lists Texas in its native range. Bell County — Fort Cavazos current INRMP identifies Chinkapin oak as a native species on the installation. Bandera County — a documented wild Texas collection from Bandera County records Q. muehlenbergii growing naturally in canyon/creek habitat. Real County — the USNVC Southern Edwards Plateau Bigtooth Maple Canyon Forest explicitly includes Q. muehlenbergii and is documented at several locations in Real County. Kerr: Singhurst et al. 2010 Kerr WMA vegetation and flora, chinkapin oak dominant in wild mesic limestone canyon woodland; voucher JS 10039, LS 4222 (p.516). Bandera, Real, Kerr meet project threshold; Bell excluded.

best_field_traits: leaf blade obovate to elliptic, usually unlobed to shallowly undulate
roughly 8–14 pairs of strong parallel secondary veins ending in regular marginal teeth
lower leaf surface pale/glaucous with minute stellate hairs
bark light to medium gray, thin and flaky/scaly
acorn matures in one season; cup commonly encloses about one-quarter to one-half of nut
Leaves usually 50–150 × 40–80 mm, leathery, obovate or sometimes narrower, margins regularly undulate/serrate, teeth often strongly antrorse (forward-pointing) but lack red-oak bristles.
Secondary lateral veins usually 10–14 near-parallel pairs reaching evenly spaced marginal teeth; look at multiple mature leaves.
Abaxial surface pale/glaucous and seemingly nearly glabrous, but minute appressed symmetric 6–10-rayed stellate hairs occur; adaxial mature blades often glossy.
Acorns commonly 1–2, sessile or on stalk up to 8 mm; cup 4–12 mm deep × 8–22 mm broad, encloses 1/4–1/2 nut; cup scales tuberculate but NOT long-fringed.
Acorn nut generally 15–20 mm long (range 13–28 mm), 1-year maturation; bur oak nuts often substantially larger.
Found on limestone/calcareous woods and canyons in the western range; occasionally stunted and shrubby in xeric terrain, so habit alone is unreliable.
morphology_keys.oak_training: Use leaf architecture plus bark/twig/buds and mature acorn/cupule; never identify an oak from leaf silhouette alone.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Quercus macrocarpa: Bur oak usually has much broader, deeply lobed or fiddle-shaped leaves and an enormous fringed cup; chinkapin oak has chestnut-like regularly toothed leaves without a deep midleaf waist. Quercus alba: White oak has obvious rounded lobes through much of the blade; chinkapin oak is primarily toothed rather than deeply lobed. Quercus michauxii: Swamp chestnut oak generally has larger leaves with coarser rounded teeth and is an East/Southeast Texas confuser rather than the typical limestone Hill Country form.

diagnostic_comparison.where_to_look_first: Compare regular forward-pointing teeth + numerous parallel veins vs a deeply waisted leaf; confirm via mature cup fringe, size, and lower-surface hairs.

pair_specific_tie_breakers.quercus-macrocarpa: Bur oak usually has a broad leaf with a dramatic pair of deep middle/proximal sinuses (waist) plus a conspicuous soft-fringed giant cup; chinkapin has a more even sequence of marginal teeth with 10–14 nearly parallel veins and smaller, non-fringed cups.

unreliable_alone: Pointed tooth tips are not the same as red-oak terminal bristles.
Western or immature bur oak acorns may have reduced fringe and overlap in cup size.
Existing chinkapin gallery's acorn photo is immature; do not mark mature cupule view complete.
Edwards Plateau Q. brayi forms are treated as clinal by FNA; do not create a separate species record solely on this label.
diagnostic_comparison.hybrid_guardrail: Use adult leaves and a mature cup, not leaf silhouette or habitat alone.
